review.overview: PR #403 adds a new `@package/queue` package. It has a transport-independent queue contract, a BullMQ adapter, an in-memory test adapter and a shared contract test suite. The scraper moves onto it: producers call `enqueueMany`, `queues.ts` holds the payload schemas and retry policy, and `processor.ts` drains through `process()` and `redriveFailed()`. The PR also stages a second Railway Redis, `pocket-trash-queue`, next to the legacy `scraper-queue`. The scraper keeps using `scraper-queue` until a later, separately approved cutover. The queue design and contract tests look sound. The main risks are the hand-written Zod payload schemas, which have no test against real producer output, and a Redis reconnect policy that is wrong for the new continuous-worker mode. The staged Redis resource also has an unclear volume binding, and the infrastructure diagrams show the new queue as live before cutover. Producer enqueue is now a serial 5-round-trip loop instead of one `addBulk`, which is a smaller cost. I found no SQL or schema changes. Reviewed against the PR file index and patches only; nothing was run.

findings.title: Hand-written Zod payload schemas are never tested against real producer output
findings.evidence: `scraperItemJobSchema` is `z.custom<ScraperItemJob>(value => scraperItemPayloadSchema.safeParse(value).success)`. `z.custom` makes the type unchecked, so nothing ties the ~150 lines of Zod schema to the `ScraperItemJob` and `ScraperImageJob` TypeScript types. The producer tests (`autmog/producer.test.ts`, `grimsmo/producer.test.ts`) replace queues with `{ enqueueMany: vi.fn() }`, so real normalized items never pass through the schema. `queues.test.ts` checks only one malformed payload and one `tmp.image.delete` job.
findings.impact: If a field differs between the normalizer output and the schema (for example `undefined` where the schema says `.nullable()`, or a new field on a source), `enqueue` throws `Invalid scraper item queue payload`. Before this PR, `addBulk` did no validation and accepted these payloads. That makes the producer run fail on the first affected item, and the first live cron run is where it would show. Jobs already waiting in Redis that no longer match would fail at delivery and burn all 5 retries.
findings.recommendation: Add a test that runs real normalizer fixtures for every item and image variant (Autmog pen, Saga catalog and materials, pen and knife variation and batch, all four image types) through `createScraperQueues(url, createInMemoryQueueAdapter()).enqueue`. Add a compile-time check so schema drift fails typecheck, for example `satisfies z.ZodType<ScraperItemJob>` on the payload schemas instead of `z.custom`.

findings.title: Redis retry policy gives up after 3 attempts, which strands continuous workers
findings.evidence: `retryStrategy(times)` returns `null` once `times > 3`, so ioredis stops reconnecting after about 1.5 seconds (250, 500 and 750 ms). The `error` handler at line 49 is empty. `processContinuously` (line 331) is added in this PR and uses the same shared connection. That path is fine for the scraper's short bounded cron, but not for a long-lived worker. No code reconnects or recreates a connection that has ended.
findings.impact: A Railway Redis restart or redeploy usually takes longer than 1.5 seconds. After it, the shared connection is permanently closed. A continuous worker (the Discord bot named in the ADR and docs) stops receiving jobs without crashing or reporting an error. Every later `enqueue` rejects, and the process keeps running until someone restarts it.
findings.recommendation: Make the retry policy depend on mode, or accept a `retryStrategy` option. For continuous use, retry indefinitely with a capped backoff. Or surface connection end through `onEvent` or a `close` callback so the host can exit and let Railway restart it. Add a test that restarts the Redis fixture while a continuous worker is open.

findings.title: Staged Redis resource has no declared volume, though docs say it uses redis-volume
findings.evidence: `sharedQueue = redis("pocket-trash-queue")` starts Redis with `--dir $RAILWAY_VOLUME_MOUNT_PATH` and AOF enabled. The only volume resource is the existing `redis-volume`, described as an existing database volume retained without changing its mount, and it is not bound to `sharedQueue`. docs/railway.md says the plan reports `1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`. It also lists the new Redis as 'Railway Redis template with `redis-volume`' and describes both apps sharing 'the 5 GB `redis-volume`'. A Railway volume mounts on one service, and that volume belongs to the legacy `scraper-queue`.
findings.impact: The planned addition provisions no volume of its own, and the legacy instance keeps `redis-volume`. If the new instance has no mount, `RAILWAY_VOLUME_MOUNT_PATH` is empty and the start command resolves to `--dir` with no value. Redis then fails to start, or runs without the RDB and AOF persistence the migration relies on. The docs also promise a 5 GB shared volume, which may not exist.
findings.recommendation: Declare a volume for `pocket-trash-queue` in the IaC, with its own size and alerts, and attach it to that service. Reword the docs so `redis-volume` stays with the legacy queue until cleanup. Step 2 of the migration (restart test for RDB and AOF) must run before any `REDIS_URL` switch. Add a check to `railway-config.test.mjs` that the new Redis has a volume.

findings.title: Infrastructure diagrams show the scraper using the new queue before cutover
findings.evidence: The prod and preview diagrams add the edges `prod_scraper -> prod_queue` (labelled scraper-images / scraper-items) and `preview_scraper -> preview_queue`, both pointing at `pocket-trash-queue` (docs/infrastructure-diagram.eraser line 40). docs/railway.md says 'the preview workflow continues to use `scraper-queue`'. The deploy workflow still sets `RAILWAY_SCRAPER_QUEUE_PREVIEW_SERVICE_NAME: scraper-queue` and builds `REDIS_URL` from its `REDIS_PUBLIC_URL`. Neither diagram shows the legacy queue.
findings.impact: The diagrams state a topology that does not exist yet. An on-call engineer reading them during an incident would look at the wrong Redis.
findings.recommendation: Draw the live edge to `scraper-queue` and show `pocket-trash-queue` as staged with no edges. Move the edges at the approved cutover.

findings.title: Producer enqueue is now serial, with 5 Redis round trips and 2 full payload reads per job
findings.evidence: Each `enqueue` does a lock `SET NX`, `getJob` (full payload), `queue.add`, a second `getJob` to read the telemetry token, and an `EVAL` to release the lock. `enqueueMany` (line 249) awaits these one at a time. The old producers did one `removeCompletedJobsById` pass and one pipelined `addBulk`. Grimsmo batch jobs carry whole item arrays, so the read-backs can pull large payloads. Expected load: a `*/5` Railway cron producing one job per catalog item plus batch jobs. I could not measure item counts.
findings.impact: Producer run time grows linearly in round trips. 1,000 jobs at about 1 ms private-network latency is roughly 5 seconds, and more if payloads are large. This is a risk for the 5-minute schedule rather than a failure today.
findings.recommendation: Measure on a real Grimsmo run. If slow, pipeline the `getJob` reads and lock acquisition for the batch, or cut the post-add `getJob` read-back by using the `add` result. Keep the per-id lock only where `replaceCompleted` is true.

findings.title: Redis usage splits across Railway config, railpack.json and the deploy workflow
findings.evidence: The install command `./scripts/pnpm-install.sh --frozen-lockfile --prefer-offline` is now written in three places: `railpack.json` (new), `RAILPACK_INSTALL_CMD` in `.railway/railway.ts` (line 105), and two new `railway variable set RAILPACK_INSTALL_CMD` steps in deploy.yml (lines 706 and 1587). The new test only checks `railpack.json`.
findings.impact: Three copies must change together. If one drifts, builds use whichever source Railpack prefers, and the failure only appears as a build-time install error in a preview or production deploy.
findings.recommendation: Keep one source of truth. If `railpack.json` is meant to cover first-time PR environments, drop the workflow `variable set` steps, or add a test asserting all three strings are identical.

findings.title: Queue integration test needs a local redis-server binary that only one CI job installs
findings.evidence: `beforeAll` spawns `redis-server`. CI adds `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install --yes redis-server` (unpinned) only before `pnpm test:ci` in one job. `packages/queue/package.json` has `test` and `test:ci` scripts and no mention of the Redis requirement.
findings.impact: `pnpm test` in a clean checkout, or any other CI job that runs the queue package, fails with `spawn redis-server ENOENT`. Each CI run also pays for an `apt-get update`.
findings.recommendation: Document the requirement in the package README or test header. Skip the integration suite with a clear message when `redis-server` is missing and `CI` is unset. Or run Redis as a CI service container and pass the URL through an env var.

findings.title: Speculative queue surface and a dangling comment
findings.evidence: The file ends with a JSDoc block, 'Checks the common envelope and job-specific data of one item payload', that documents no function. In `packages/queue`, the scraper uses only `mode: "bounded"` and never passes `onEvent`. `processContinuously`, the lifecycle events, and the continuous-worker branch of the in-memory adapter have no production caller in this PR.
findings.impact: The orphan comment is dead text left behind by the rewrite. The unused surface adds about 150 lines that must be maintained and tested before any app uses it, and the reconnect problem above lives in exactly that surface.
findings.recommendation: Delete the orphan comment. Keep the continuous path if the Discord bot lands next, but note it in the ADR as staged. Otherwise remove it until a consumer exists.

review.overview: PR #354 adds the Pens catalog schema: pen and pen-part subtypes, refills and offerings, compatibility claims, market lifecycle, source evidence, product configuration slots, and owned-item configuration. It also reworks catalog_terminology_alias onto a new catalog_terminology_concept table. The schema is carefully constrained, with composite foreign keys, CHECK constraints, and deferred constraint triggers. The main risks are in those triggers and the alias migration. Many trigger functions scan whole tables for every changed row. The alias trigger can fail on legacy rows that were never validated. 'An owned part is installed only once' is enforced by a trigger and is not safe under concurrent transactions. Product types are copied into concepts once, with no ongoing sync. The migration was read but not run, and no existing production data was available.

findings.title: Deferred constraint triggers re-scan whole tables for every changed row
findings.evidence: validate_refill_supporting_evidence() is attached with FOR EACH ROW to 11 tables (lines 1049-1058). Each call runs five NOT EXISTS checks over all of refill_offering, refill_offering_market_status, refill_offering_identifier, refill_compatibility_group_membership and refill_compatibility_assertion. validate_refill_market_conflicts() (line 1066) builds a recursive closure over all of catalog_market and self-joins all active statuses and identifiers, per row. validate_product_configuration() (line 844), validate_catalog_terminology_aliases() (line 814) and validate_collection_configuration_selections() (line 933) also check the whole table and ignore NEW/OLD.
findings.impact: Cost grows as rows changed times table size. A bulk catalog import, scraper run or admin load of N offerings or evidence links costs about N times the table size in scans, all at COMMIT. Imports will slow sharply as the catalog grows. Because the checks are table-wide, one bad row from any earlier transaction blocks every later write to the same tables, including unrelated rows.
findings.recommendation: Scope each check to the row that changed: use NEW.id/OLD.id, or the parent id for link tables, as in validate_pens_product_detail(). For the market-closure check, restrict the recursion to the affected offering or maker. Alternatively, run the whole-table audit once in the migration and in tests. Add a bulk-insert test with a few thousand rows to catch regressions.

findings.title: Alias collision trigger can reject writes because of legacy rows that were never checked
findings.evidence: The backfill UPDATE of catalog_terminology_alias.concept_id (line 558) runs before the constraint trigger is created (line 834), so existing aliases are never validated. The pre-flight audit (lines 486-496) only checks for the same value mapping to different canonical keys. It does not check for an alias equal to a concept's key or normalized label. The trigger body checks every row in catalog_terminology_alias, not only NEW.
findings.impact: If production holds an alias such as 'spinner' for the spinner concept, every later alias insert or update fails at commit with 'Terminology alias collides with a canonical term'. This includes changes to unrelated aliases. Admin alias management would be blocked until someone fixes the old row by hand.
findings.recommendation: Add the same canonical-term collision query to the DO $$ audit block before the trigger exists, so the migration fails early and names the bad rows. Alternatively, delete or rewrite the colliding aliases in the migration. Also scope the trigger to NEW.id.

findings.title: 'Owned part installed only once' is trigger-only and can be bypassed by concurrent transactions
findings.evidence: validate_collection_configuration_selections() rejects an installed_part_collection_item_id used by more than one selection via GROUP BY ... HAVING count(*) > 1 (lines 956-963). The trigger is deferred, so it runs at COMMIT and sees only committed rows. The column only has a plain index (collection_item_configuration_selection_installed_part_idx, line 589). It has no unique index.
findings.impact: Under READ COMMITTED, two transactions that install the same owned clip into two different pens both commit without error, because neither sees the other's uncommitted row. The invariant breaks silently, and the collection UI would show one physical part installed in two pens.
findings.recommendation: Replace the trigger check with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON collection_item_configuration_selection (installed_part_collection_item_id) WHERE installed_part_collection_item_id IS NOT NULL. Mirror it with uniqueIndex().where(...) in pens.ts. Delete the duplicate trigger branch.

findings.title: Product-type concepts are copied once and never kept in sync
findings.evidence: The migration drops the foreign key from catalog_terminology_alias.canonical_key to product_types.slug (line 483). It then seeds catalog_terminology_concept from product_types in a one-time INSERT ... SELECT (lines 514-523). createTerminologyAlias now throws 'Catalog terminology concept does not exist.' when no concept row exists (packages/services/src/db/catalog/index.ts:2458). The updated service test must insert the concept by hand after inserting a product type (packages/services/src/db/catalog/index.integration.test.ts, +58-64).
findings.impact: A product type added later through a scraper import, admin tooling or a future migration has no concept, so aliases for it cannot be created. Renaming a product type leaves the concept label stale. Deleting a product type no longer fails on aliases, and the concept stays behind. The previous foreign key guaranteed these cases stayed consistent.
findings.recommendation: Keep the two in sync in the database with an AFTER INSERT/UPDATE trigger on product_types that upserts the product-type concept. Alternatively, have the service create the concept in the same transaction when it is missing. Add a test that inserts a product type and then creates an alias for it with no manual concept insert.

findings.title: Alias listing drops global aliases and can throw on new product-type concepts
findings.evidence: The schema now allows maker_id IS NULL (global aliases) and seeds concepts for pen, pen-clip, refill and other new product types. listTerminologyAliases() still uses innerJoin(schema.maker, ...), so global aliases are silently dropped. The new 'lost its maker' throw after that join can never run. catalogProductType() accepts only the five slider and spinner slugs and throws 'Unsupported catalog product type' for anything else (lines 252-262).
findings.impact: A global alias is invisible in the admin list. A single alias on a 'pen' concept, which the schema permits, makes the whole list call throw and breaks the admin terminology page.
findings.recommendation: Use leftJoin on maker and return makerId: number | null in the CatalogTerminologyAlias type, or filter to maker-scoped rows in SQL (where makerId is not null). Skip rows whose concept key is outside the supported product types, or widen the type. Remove the unreachable throw.

findings.title: Conflict message no longer matches the widened unique constraint
findings.evidence: The mapped constraint is now catalog_terminology_alias_scope_value_unique, which is UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (maker_id, canonical_namespace, normalized_value). It no longer includes the concept. The message still says 'Alias already exists for this maker and concept.'
findings.impact: If an admin adds an alias that already points to a different concept for the same maker, the error blames the wrong concept and gives no hint about what to fix.
findings.recommendation: Change the text to 'Alias already exists for this maker and namespace.' or similar.

findings.title: Integration tests skip several trigger-enforced invariants
findings.evidence: The tests cover product subtype checks, slot kinds and rule order, alias collision, market cycles, evidence-required approval, append-only evidence, successor scope and overlapping markets. No test touches validate_collection_configuration_selections() (wrong product slot, installed part owner or choice mismatch, double install). No test covers validate_pen_nose_profile_carrier(), the dimensional-comparison or physical-fit-test branches of refill_compatibility_evidence_fields_valid, refill-identifier market conflicts, or the migration backfill on a database that already contains aliases.
findings.impact: The owned-item configuration trigger and the alias backfill are the riskiest new write paths and have no failing test if they break. The alias backfill is also where legacy data can break the migration.
findings.recommendation: Add one test per untested trigger with a rejected case. Add a migration test that seeds aliases on the pre-migration schema and applies this migration. Cover the concurrent double-install case once the unique index is added.

blockingFindingsForAdjudication.title: Deferred constraint triggers re-scan whole tables for every changed row
blockingFindingsForAdjudication.evidence: validate_refill_supporting_evidence() is attached with FOR EACH ROW to 11 tables (lines 1049-1058). Each call runs five NOT EXISTS checks over all of refill_offering, refill_offering_market_status, refill_offering_identifier, refill_compatibility_group_membership and refill_compatibility_assertion. validate_refill_market_conflicts() (line 1066) builds a recursive closure over all of catalog_market and self-joins all active statuses and identifiers, per row. validate_product_configuration() (line 844), validate_catalog_terminology_aliases() (line 814) and validate_collection_configuration_selections() (line 933) also check the whole table and ignore NEW/OLD.
blockingFindingsForAdjudication.impact: Cost grows as rows changed times table size. A bulk catalog import, scraper run or admin load of N offerings or evidence links costs about N times the table size in scans, all at COMMIT. Imports will slow sharply as the catalog grows. Because the checks are table-wide, one bad row from any earlier transaction blocks every later write to the same tables, including unrelated rows.
blockingFindingsForAdjudication.recommendation: Scope each check to the row that changed: use NEW.id/OLD.id, or the parent id for link tables, as in validate_pens_product_detail(). For the market-closure check, restrict the recursion to the affected offering or maker. Alternatively, run the whole-table audit once in the migration and in tests. Add a bulk-insert test with a few thousand rows to catch regressions.

review.overview: PR #354 adds the Pens catalog schema: 45 new tables, a migration with seed data and 20 trigger functions, and a rework of terminology aliases onto a new concept table. The table design is careful, with composite foreign keys and check constraints. The weak spots are the triggers and the unvalidated links. One trigger re-scans the whole user-written selection table on every row write (high). Another enforces 'one installed part' without a unique index, so concurrent writes can both pass. Source-listing links can cross products and makers. Product deletion does not know about Pens references. The riskiest logic has no tests. I assumed many users writing collection data and occasional bulk imports of catalog data. I did not run the migration or the tests.

findings.title: Selection trigger re-validates the whole user table on every row write
findings.evidence: validate_collection_configuration_selections() is a FOR EACH ROW deferred trigger on collection_item_configuration_selection (line 966). It never uses NEW or OLD. It joins every selection row to its slot, calls collection_catalog_product() on each (an 11-branch UNION ALL, lines 918-932), and runs a GROUP BY over the whole table (lines 956-961).
findings.impact: This table holds user data and grows with every configured pen. Each commit that touches k rows does k full scans, each costing N times 11 index lookups. At 100k selections one save costs well over a million lookups, and an import or bulk edit is quadratic. Any old bad row also makes every later write fail, whoever owns it.
findings.recommendation: Scope each check to the affected row, e.g. WHERE selection.collection_item_id = COALESCE(NEW.collection_item_id, OLD.collection_item_id). Check the installed-part count only for the new installed_part_collection_item_id. Do the same in every other trigger that scans a whole table.

findings.title: 'Installed only once' is a trigger check, so two concurrent writes can both pass
findings.evidence: The rule that an owned part is installed once is a GROUP BY ... HAVING count(*) > 1 inside a deferred trigger. collection_item_configuration_selection only has a plain index on installed_part_collection_item_id (pens.ts:745). The existing spinner and slider code uses unique indexes for the same rule (collection_detail_spinner_installed_button_unique, collection_detail_slider_installed_plate_unique).
findings.impact: Under READ COMMITTED, two transactions can install the same part into two pens. Each trigger sees only its own uncommitted row, so both commit and the part ends up in two pens.
findings.recommendation: Add a unique index on installed_part_collection_item_id (WHERE it is not null) and delete the GROUP BY branch. Keep the trigger only for the cross-table owner and product checks.

findings.title: Catalog validation triggers scan whole tables and one bad row blocks unrelated writes
findings.evidence: validate_refill_supporting_evidence() runs five NOT EXISTS scans over all offerings, statuses, identifiers, memberships and assertions. It is attached to 14 row-level triggers (lines 1049-1058). validate_product_configuration(), validate_product_configuration_rules(), validate_catalog_terminology_aliases(), validate_pen_nose_profile_carrier() and validate_refill_market_conflicts() also ignore NEW and OLD. The alias trigger (lines 814-834) rejects any alias equal to a canonical key or label. The migration audit (lines 486-496) checks only cross-concept duplicates.
findings.impact: A curated import of N rows costs about N full scans at commit. A legacy alias that matches a canonical label, e.g. 'Slider Insert' for key slider-insert, makes every later alias insert fail with 'collides with a canonical term', even for other makers.
findings.recommendation: Filter each function by the id in NEW or OLD, or by the parent id of the touched row. Extend the migration audit to cover the alias-versus-canonical-label rule so bad rows surface during migration, not at the next unrelated write.

findings.title: Source listing links can point at other products and makers
findings.evidence: catalog_source_listing_choice(listing_id, choice_id) has two independent foreign keys. catalog_source_image (line 900) links listing_id and product_image_id independently. product_source_listing (line 867) links product_id and listing_id independently, and the listing's maker_id is never compared with the product's. The PR adds product_id_maker_unique and composite foreign keys for refills, but not here. No trigger covers these tables.
findings.impact: A listing mapped to product A can carry a configuration choice or image of product B, or belong to a different maker. Wrong provenance gets shown with no error.
findings.recommendation: Carry product_id and maker_id on these link rows and use composite foreign keys: (product_id, maker_id) to product, (listing_id, maker_id) to the listing, (choice_id, product_id) to the choice, and (product_image_id, product_id) to the image (each needs a matching unique key).

findings.title: The riskiest new logic has no test
findings.evidence: The suite never touches collection_item_configuration_selection, validate_collection_configuration_selections(), collection_catalog_product(), the nose-profile carrier trigger, pen_part_role_assignment, the concept-key immutability trigger, product_source_listing, catalog_source_listing_choice, or catalog_source_image. It only runs migrate() on an empty database (line 43).
findings.impact: The owner check, product match and installed-part match have no failing test. The migration steps that move existing alias rows to concept_id (backfill, NOT NULL, dropped canonical_key) never see existing data.
findings.recommendation: Add one test per rejection path for the selection trigger. Add one upgrade test that migrates to the previous migration, inserts aliases, then applies this migration and checks concept_id.

findings.title: Product delete guard ignores the new Pens references
findings.evidence: deleteProduct documents that referenced products stay unchanged and it returns false. Its reference query lists only spinner and slider tables (lines 3293-3300), and it locks only spinner and slider subtypes (lines 3266-3286). The PR adds many ON DELETE RESTRICT references to Pen products: collection_detail_pen*.product_pen_*_id, refill_offering via product_detail_refill, product_source_listing, pen_part_role_assignment, product_configuration_choice.part_product_id, and compatibility rows.
findings.impact: Deleting a Pen or refill product that someone owns or that has offerings gets past the guard. The cascade into the detail row then hits a RESTRICT, and the call throws a raw foreign-key error instead of returning false. Pen subtype rows are also not locked, so a concurrent writer can slip a reference in.
findings.recommendation: Add the Pens reference tables to the guard query and lock the Pens subtype rows like the spinner and slider ones. Add a test that deleting an owned Pen returns false.

findings.title: Concept rows are not tied to product_types
findings.evidence: The old foreign key from the alias canonical_key to product_types.slug is dropped (migration line 483). Concept rows for product-type are copied once at migration time (lines 514-523). Nothing creates a concept when a product type is added later. The updated test inserts the concept by hand (index.integration.test.ts:152).
findings.impact: A product type added after this migration cannot get aliases. createTerminologyAlias throws 'Catalog terminology concept does not exist.', where before the foreign key made it work.
findings.recommendation: Create the concept in the same code path or migration that adds a product type, or add a trigger on product_types that inserts it.

findings.title: Seed upserts overwrite staff-edited rows
findings.evidence: The product_types seed uses ON CONFLICT (slug) DO UPDATE SET name and is_part_or_accessory. mechanisms, configuration_slot_kind and catalog_market are overwritten the same way. The service has setProductTypePartOrAccessory, so staff can change is_part_or_accessory.
findings.impact: If production already has a row with slug 'refill' or 'pen' that staff edited, the migration resets it without any notice.
findings.recommendation: Use DO NOTHING for rows staff may have edited, or fail the migration when an existing row differs from the seed.

findings.title: Unused unique constraints and redundant indexes add write cost
findings.evidence: Four composite unique constraints are never referenced by a foreign key: refill_offering_market_status_id_scope_unique (980), refill_offering_identifier_id_scope_unique (1058), product_configuration_choice_id_slot_product_unique (416), product_configuration_choice_rule_id_target_product_unique (472). Four indexes repeat the leading columns of an existing unique key: product_detail_refill_maker_id_idx (148), refill_offering_refill_idx (582), product_alias_product_id_idx (226), catalog_source_listing_source_idx (817).
findings.impact: Each extra index is kept up to date on every write and needs vacuum for no read benefit.
findings.recommendation: Drop the eight objects. Re-add a constraint only when a composite foreign key needs it.

findings.title: Nullable alias maker has no code path, with dead code and a wrong message
findings.evidence: catalog_terminology_alias.maker_id becomes nullable, with a preferred-scope check and NULLS NOT DISTINCT. createTerminologyAlias always sets a maker. listTerminologyAliases inner-joins maker (line 3600), so the null check at line 3609 cannot run. The conflict message 'Alias already exists for this maker and concept.' (line 177) now also fires when the same alias maps to a different concept.
findings.impact: Global aliases would be invisible in the list. The error text misleads staff, and the unused branch adds code to read and maintain.
findings.recommendation: Keep maker_id NOT NULL until a global-alias feature exists. If it stays, left-join maker and reword the message to 'for this maker and namespace'.

findings.title: Installed-part uniqueness can be broken by concurrent writes
findings.evidence: 'An owned Pen part may be installed only once' is checked by a GROUP BY inside a deferred trigger (lines 956-963). collection.ts uses a partial unique index for the same rule on spinners and sliders (collection_detail_spinner_installed_button_unique, collection_detail_slider_installed_plate_unique). Under READ COMMITTED, each of two concurrent transactions checks at commit and does not see the other's uncommitted row.
findings.impact: Two sessions can install the same owned part into two different pens, and both commits succeed. The invariant breaks silently and the duplicate shows up later as inconsistent inventory.
findings.recommendation: Add CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON collection_item_configuration_selection (installed_part_collection_item_id) WHERE installed_part_collection_item_id IS NOT NULL, as in the existing pattern. Then delete the duplicate-install block from the trigger.

findings.title: Installed part uses ON DELETE RESTRICT, unlike the existing pattern
findings.evidence: installed_part_collection_item_id references collection_item with onDelete restrict. The spinner and slider installed-part columns use onDelete set null (collection.ts lines 1084-1088 and 1142-1152). collection_item.owner_id cascades from users. When a user is deleted, pen A and part B both go in one cascade. The RESTRICT check for B runs when B's delete event is processed, and A's selection row is removed when A's event is processed. If B is processed first, the check finds A's selection and fails. No test deletes a user or a part that is installed. I did not run this.
findings.impact: Deleting an owned part that is installed is blocked. Deleting a user who has an installed part may fail depending on row order, which would also affect account erasure.
findings.recommendation: Use ON DELETE SET NULL for installed_part_collection_item_id, matching spinner and slider. Add a test that deletes a user whose pen has an installed part, and one that deletes the part itself.

findings.title: New product types cannot get aliases: concepts are not kept in sync
findings.evidence: createTerminologyAlias now looks up a catalog_terminology_concept row and throws 'Catalog terminology concept does not exist.' if none is found. The migration copies product_types into concepts once (lines 514-523). Nothing links the two tables afterwards. The old FK from canonical_key to product_types.slug guaranteed a match. The updated test has to insert a concept by hand for 'slider-insert' (catalog/index.integration.test.ts lines 147-158). I did not find the production product-type creation path in this diff.
findings.impact: Any product type created after this migration cannot get aliases until someone inserts a concept row by hand. Renaming a product type leaves the concept's label snapshot stale, and the alias collision trigger checks that stale label.
findings.recommendation: Create the concept in the same transaction that creates the product type, or add an AFTER INSERT trigger on product_types. Alternatively, have the alias service create the missing 'product-type' concept. Add a test that creates a product type through the normal path and then an alias.

findings.title: One legacy alias can block every later alias write
findings.evidence: validate_catalog_terminology_aliases scans all aliases, not just NEW. It raises if any alias equals its own concept's key or normalized label (lines 825-831). The migration's DO block (lines 486-496) only checks for duplicate (maker, namespace, normalized_value) across different keys. It does not check existing aliases against the new canonical-term rule. Concrete case: an existing alias 'Spinner' for product type 'spinner' loads without error.
findings.impact: After the migration, inserting or updating any unrelated alias fails with 'Terminology alias collides with a canonical term' until the old row is found and fixed. The error does not name the offending row.
findings.recommendation: Add a pre-flight audit in the migration that raises for existing aliases matching their concept key or label, and list the ids. Also scope the trigger to NEW.id so one bad row cannot block unrelated writes.

findings.title: Tests skip the owner-facing selection path and the upgrade path
findings.evidence: The suite covers subtype consistency, slot and rule checks, the alias collision, markets, evidence and successors. Nothing inserts into collection_item_configuration_selection, so validate_collection_configuration_selections and collection_catalog_product have no test. Nothing covers installed-part ownership, double install, pen_nose_profile_assignment carrier rules, or concept key immutability. The suite migrates a fresh database only, so the alias backfill (migration lines 557-565) never runs on existing alias rows.
findings.impact: The trigger that runs on user writes, and the data migration that can fail on real data, ship with no test that fails when they break. A column typo in plpgsql bodies would only appear at runtime, because PostgreSQL does not check them at CREATE FUNCTION.
findings.recommendation: Add tests that: reject a slot from another product; reject a part owned by another user; reject double install; reject a nose profile on a non-pen product; reject a concept key update. Add one upgrade test that seeds the previous schema with an alias row, then runs the new migration.

findings.title: Migration overwrites existing lookup rows and has no name-conflict pre-check
findings.evidence: INSERT INTO product_types ... ON CONFLICT (slug) DO UPDATE sets name and is_part_or_accessory (lines 497-508). mechanisms does the same for name (lines 509-513). The concept backfill only handles conflicts on (namespace, key). It can still fail on the (namespace, normalized_canonical_label) unique constraint if two product types share a lowercased name.
findings.impact: If production already has a 'pen', 'refill' or 'click' row that was edited by an admin, the migration silently reverts those edits. A label collision aborts the whole migration part-way through the deploy.
findings.recommendation: Use DO NOTHING for existing slugs, or audit and raise if name or flags differ. Add a pre-check for label collisions in the concept backfill.

findings.title: Unused unique constraints and redundant indexes add write cost
findings.evidence: No FK targets these unique constraints: product_configuration_choice_id_slot_product_unique (line 416), product_configuration_choice_rule_id_target_product_unique (472), refill_offering_market_status_id_scope_unique (980) and refill_offering_identifier_id_scope_unique (1058). These indexes duplicate a leading unique column: product_alias_product_id_idx, refill_offering_refill_idx, product_detail_refill_maker_id_idx, catalog_source_listing_source_idx.
findings.impact: About 8 extra indexes are maintained on every insert and update, and each is one more thing to read and keep in sync.
findings.recommendation: Drop the four unused uniques, or use them for the composite successor FKs. Drop the four duplicate indexes. Roughly 10 lines and 8 indexes go away.

blockingFindingsForAdjudication.title: Constraint triggers rescan whole tables on every row change
blockingFindingsForAdjudication.evidence: validate_collection_configuration_selections (lines 933-966) has no filter on NEW or OLD. It joins every row of collection_item_configuration_selection and calls collection_catalog_product, an 11-table UNION ALL, once per row. It then runs GROUP BY over the whole table. It is a deferred FOR EACH ROW trigger, so it runs once per changed row at commit. The same pattern appears in validate_refill_supporting_evidence (line 1012, fired by 10 triggers, scans 5 tables), validate_refill_market_conflicts (1066), validate_product_configuration (844), validate_pen_nose_profile_carrier (800) and validate_catalog_terminology_aliases (814).
blockingFindingsForAdjudication.impact: Each write costs time proportional to the total rows in the table, across all users. I assumed about 100k selection rows. One user saving a pen configuration then does about 1.1M index probes at commit, and a user delete with K selections repeats that K times. A bulk import of N approved refill rows runs 5 table scans N times. Commits get slow and transactions stay open longer.
blockingFindingsForAdjudication.recommendation: Scope every check to the touched row with NEW.id or OLD.id, or its parent key. Replace trigger-only rules with declarative ones where possible. For successor scope, add a composite FK (successor_id, offering_id, market_id) to (id, offering_id, market_id). The refill_offering_market_status_id_scope_unique and refill_offering_identifier_id_scope_unique constraints already exist for this and nothing uses them. For installed parts, use a partial unique index.

review.overview: This PR adds material drill-downs to the public Trends page. A new service method returns exact catalog-product counts by material, product type and specific alloy. The generation refresh now also stores privacy-filtered, rounded item and collector counts in a new table, public_collection_item_material_trend. Each row needs at least 5 distinct owners, and counts are rounded to the nearest 5. The page gets material and specific-material filters stored in the URL. The privacy threshold, rounding, atomic generation swap and the specific-parent foreign key look correct. The findings are an inflated 'Other' bar, a gap between deploy and the first refresh, dead rows and duplicated payload, and thin tests for the new filter logic. I assumed a public, unauthenticated page with a catalog of a few thousand products.

findings.title: 'Other' material bar adds up overlapping counts
findings.evidence: MaterialTrendVisualization builds the Other bar with `overflow.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value.count, 0)` over every material row after the eighth. The service counts a product or item once under every material it has (see the doc comment at packages/services/src/db/trends/index.ts:123). Collector counts are distinct per material row, so one collector who owns items in several materials appears in each row.
findings.impact: A product that is Steel and Titanium counts twice if both fall into the overflow. A collector with items in three overflow materials counts three times. The Other bar can exceed the real number of distinct products, items or collectors, and the chart and table disagree on what the number means. The product-type version of this code does not have the problem because each item has one product type.
findings.recommendation: Drop the summed Other bucket for materials and show the top 8 rows with the full table below. Or compute a distinct 'all other materials' count in SQL. Or label the bar so it is clear that it is not a distinct count.

findings.title: Material section shows 'empty' until the next refresh after deploy
findings.evidence: The migration adds `has_suppressed_material_values boolean DEFAULT false NOT NULL` to public_trends_generation (migration.sql:14). The already-active generation has no rows in public_collection_item_material_trend. getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends returns a non-null object with empty arrays. The page then picks `materialsEmpty` because hasSuppressedValues is false. The 'unavailable' alert only shows when the result is null.
findings.impact: From deploy until refreshPublicCollectionItemTrends next runs, visitors see 'no values yet' for collection materials. The data is not missing; it has not been generated. The stale flag only trips after 36 hours.
findings.recommendation: Run a refresh as part of the deploy. Or have getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends return null when the active generation has no material rows and no suppressed flag, so the existing 'unavailable' state shows.

findings.title: Unused rows are stored and the payload is sent three times
findings.evidence: The second grouping set (product type, material, specific) produces `isSpecificBreakdown = true` even when `material_specific_id` is null. For materials with no specific, this repeats the first set. For the Unspecified bucket (`material_id` null) it produces an extra row that filterMaterials in trends-page.tsx:227-238 can never match, because specific mode requires a materialId. The same rows are mapped twice (collectorValues and itemValues, lines 264-287). The route loader sends them to the browser alongside the catalog rows, and filtering happens in the client. getPublicCatalogMaterialTrends (line 128) runs on every request with no cache.
findings.impact: Table size and page payload grow with product types × materials × specifics, with each row stored twice and sent three times. Every anonymous page view runs a count(distinct) aggregate over product and product_material. This is fine at a few hundred rows. It is wasted work as the catalog grows.
findings.recommendation: Filter the unused rows in SQL, for example by adding `having scoped_items.material_id is not null or grouping(...) <> 0`. Send one row array with both counts instead of two copies. Cache the catalog query, or filter by productTypeId and materialId on the server.

findings.title: Refresh runs the same item scan twice
findings.evidence: The 11-way `item_products` union CTE is copied in full at lines 427-439 and again at 491-502. The product-type query and the material query both join collection_item, product and product_types with the same filters. The second query is a superset, because it left-joins product_material and uses grouping sets.
findings.impact: The refresh holds an advisory lock and a transaction while it scans every collection detail table twice. Adding a twelfth detail table means editing two lists, and missing one makes the two result sets disagree without any error.
findings.recommendation: Define the item_products SQL once, as a shared SQL fragment or a temp table inside the transaction. Better, derive the product-type totals from the same pass.

findings.title: Restricting foreign keys have no supporting index
findings.evidence: The foreign keys on product_type_id, material_id and (material_id, material_specific_id) use ON DELETE RESTRICT (lines 17-19). The only index on the table is the unique index that starts with generation_id (line 15), which cannot serve lookups by those columns. The refresh never deletes old generations in the code shown, so rows accumulate with every refresh.
findings.impact: Deleting a product type, material or specific scans the whole table to check for referencing rows. The cost grows with each retained generation. This is a rare admin operation, so the risk is small.
findings.recommendation: Add indexes on product_type_id and (material_id, material_specific_id), or confirm that old generations are pruned elsewhere so the table stays small.

findings.title: New filter and overflow logic is untested
findings.evidence: The one new page test passes a single specific-breakdown row with only materialId set. Nothing covers filterMaterials (trends-page.tsx:227-238) for the specific-material filter, the product-type filter combined with a material filter, Unspecified rows, the more-than-8-rows Other bar, or the empty and suppressed states of the new section. The parseCatalogTrendsSearch changes get 18 added lines in catalog-filters.test.ts, which this review did not read in full.
findings.impact: The `isSpecificBreakdown === Boolean(materialId)` rule ties the page to the SQL grouping-set flag. A change to either side would silently empty the charts, and no test would fail.
findings.recommendation: Add one page test with rows from both grouping sets. It should cover headline, material-selected, specific-selected and more-than-8-rows cases, and assert the visible labels and counts.

review.overview: PR #376 adds material drill-downs to the public Trends page. It has an exact catalog material query, a new privacy-filtered `public_collection_item_material_trend` table filled by the existing refresh transaction, URL filters for material and specific material, and UI charts and tables. The migration is additive and the rounding and threshold logic looks correct. The main gaps are a missing test for material-level privacy suppression, unordered reads, an uncached catalog query on a public route, and unbounded row growth per generation.

findings.title: No test proves that small material buckets are suppressed
findings.evidence: The fixture gives Steel and Titanium exactly five owners each. Every material bucket is at or above the threshold, so the new `publishableMaterials` filter in `refreshPublicCollectionItemTrends` never drops a material row. `hasSuppressedValues: true` in the material assertion comes from the product-type data, because the Spinner type has four owners.
findings.impact: The privacy rule for materials is the core of this feature. If someone changes the `contributorCount >= PUBLIC_TRENDS_CONTRIBUTOR_THRESHOLD` filter on materials or specifics, no test fails. Counts from fewer than five collectors could then be published.
findings.recommendation: Add a fixture with a material or specific (for example an alloy used by only 4 owners). Assert that no stored row exists for it and that `hasSuppressedMaterialValues` is true. Add one case where the general material passes and one of its specifics is dropped.

findings.title: Material rows are read without ORDER BY, and the test relies on row order
findings.evidence: `getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends` selects from `public_collection_item_material_trend` with two left joins and no `orderBy`. Its siblings `getPublicPartAccessoryTrends` and `getPublicCollectionItemTrends` both order by count and name. The integration test uses `toEqual([Steel, Titanium])`, and both rows have count 10, so the expected order depends on how Postgres happens to return them.
findings.impact: Rows with equal counts can appear in a different order from one load to the next. The integration test can fail without any code change after a planner or PGlite version change.
findings.recommendation: Add `.orderBy(desc(roundedItemCount), asc(schema.material.name), asc(schema.materialSpecific.name))` to the query. Keep the test's expected order.

findings.title: Catalog material query runs uncached on every public Trends request
findings.evidence: `getPublicCatalogMaterialTrends` is called from the `/trends` loader (`apps/web/src/routes/trends.tsx`). Each call scans every approved product joined to `product_material`. It then unions two scopes and computes `count(distinct ...)` over two grouping sets. It returns every product-type x material x specific row, and the loader serializes all of them to the client.
findings.impact: An anonymous page now triggers a heavier query on each request, and the payload grows with the number of types, materials and alloys. This is fine at small catalog size. It becomes a cheap way to load the database as the catalog grows. The collection-side data is already precomputed.
findings.recommendation: Short-term, cache the result for a few minutes in the server function. Longer-term, compute it in the same refresh job and store it with the generation. Alternatively, return only the rows for the current URL filter.

findings.title: Old generations are kept, and each one now stores a large material table
findings.evidence: Each refresh inserts a new generation and deactivates the old one. It never deletes old ones. The test asserts that two generations remain after two refreshes. The new table stores one row for each product type, material and specific combination that passes the threshold, for every generation.
findings.impact: Rows grow linearly with each refresh. Old rows are never read, because the read path filters on the active generation only. The growth is slow but unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Delete generations other than the new active one (or all but the last N) at the end of the refresh transaction. The `ON DELETE CASCADE` foreign keys already remove the child rows.

findings.title: Active generation has no material rows until the next refresh after deploy
findings.evidence: The migration creates an empty material table. It adds `has_suppressed_material_values` with default false. Nothing backfills the generation that is already active.
findings.impact: From deploy until the next refresh, `getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends` returns a non-null generation with zero rows. The page shows the plain 'materials empty' message with no suppression note and no error state.
findings.recommendation: Trigger a refresh as part of the release, or note it in the release steps. Alternatively, have the read path return null when the active generation has no material rows.

findings.title: The 11-table collection union runs twice in one refresh
findings.evidence: The `item_products` CTE (11 `union all` branches) is repeated in the product-type query at line 427 and again in the new material query at line 491. Both run inside the same transaction while holding the advisory lock.
findings.impact: The refresh does the same scan twice. If a twelfth detail table is added, it must be edited in both places or one of the two result sets will quietly miss it.
findings.recommendation: Move the CTE text into one shared `sql` fragment used by both queries. Optionally, derive the product-type counts from the material query's rows.

review.overview: PR #376 adds material drill-downs to the public Trends page. It adds exact catalog material counts, computed live from approved products. It also adds privacy-filtered collection material counts, stored per generation in a new table, public_collection_item_material_trend. Rows are kept only when at least 5 distinct owners contribute, and counts are rounded to the nearest 5. The migration, schema, refresh transaction, URL filters, and UI are consistent with each other. I found no blocking bug. The count constraints hold because contributorCount >= 5 and itemCount >= contributorCount. The grouping-set flags (isSpecificBreakdown) and the unique index with coalesce also match the schema. The remaining findings are low severity: a live uncached public query, a weak spot in the privacy design, and duplicated payload.

findings.title: Exact catalog material query runs uncached on every public Trends load
findings.evidence: getPublicCatalogMaterialTrends runs a live query on each call. It joins product, product_types and product_material, unions the eligible rows twice (headline scope plus per-product-type scope), and runs count(distinct id) over two grouping sets. The route loader (apps/web/src/routes/trends.tsx:42) calls it for every anonymous /trends request. The collection material data, by contrast, is precomputed per generation.
findings.impact: Cost grows with the number of approved products times their materials, and it is paid on every page view by anonymous traffic. Many concurrent requests would each repeat the same aggregate. I assumed a public, unauthenticated page with no per-route caching, and found no cache in the PR. The catalog size is not known.
findings.recommendation: Cache the result for a short time at the server-function or HTTP layer. Alternatively, compute it in the same refresh transaction as the collection data and store it per generation. This matters most if the catalog grows large.

findings.title: Suppressed material buckets can be inferred by subtraction
findings.evidence: Each row is suppressed on its own when its contributorCount is below 5. The headline rows (productTypeId null) and the per-product-type rows are published for the same generation. The general-material row and the specific-material rows are published together too. No complementary suppression is applied, so a suppressed child bucket can be derived from a published parent. The generation also exposes hasSuppressedValues, which tells readers that a bucket was removed.
findings.impact: Example: headline Titanium shows 20 items, and the published per-type rows for Titanium sum to 15. The 5-item remainder belongs to a type or alloy with fewer than 5 owners. Rounding to 5 blurs the number but does not remove it. A small group's holdings can therefore be partly recovered. This is the same shape as the existing product-type design, so it may be an accepted trade-off.
findings.recommendation: If the 5-owner rule must hold for derived values, suppress the parent total or a sibling whenever exactly one child is suppressed. Otherwise, document the accepted risk next to PUBLIC_TRENDS_CONTRIBUTOR_THRESHOLD.

findings.title: Collection material rows are mapped twice and sent whole to every client
findings.evidence: getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends builds collectorValues and itemValues from the same rows. Both arrays carry identical material identity fields (name, slug, ids), and only count differs. The route loader returns both arrays to the page for all product-type, material and specific combinations. The page then filters them in the browser (filterMaterials in trends-page.tsx).
findings.impact: The serialized loader payload carries every material identity field twice. It grows with product types times materials times specifics. This is fine at small scale, but it adds avoidable bytes to a public page.
findings.recommendation: Return one row list with itemCount and collectorCount on each row, and let the page pick the count for each chart. This removes about 15 lines of duplicate mapping and halves the payload.
